newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arabs travel Hebron road closed since '94 massacre.
newsitem.headline: Arabs travel Hebron road closed since '94 massacre.

text.p: Israel, under a U.S.-brokered peace deal with the PLO, opened a main road in the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian traffic on Monday for the first time since a 1994 massacre.

Witnesses said ambulances, taxis and municipal vehicles began trickling through a section of Shuhada, or Martyrs, street once Israeli police and soldiers opened it to traffic around 7.30 a.m. (0530 GMT).
Israel handed over 80 percent of Hebron to PLO rule on January 17. The street borders Jewish settlements in the 20 percent of Hebron still under Israeli control.

The street, closed to Palestinian vehicles since Jewish settler Baruch Goldstein massacred 29 Arab worshippers at al-Ibrahimi mosque in February 1994, will reopen in stages over a four-month period under the peace deal.

Israeli soldiers stopped one of the first half dozen or so vehicles -- a taxi -- and told the driver he needed a permit from the Israeli civil administration occupation authorities to travel the road, witnesses said.

Palestinians had demanded the reopening of the street which abuts an old vegetable market. Some 400 Jewish settlers, who opposed the Hebron handover, and 20,000 Arabs live on the Israeli-held side of the volatile town.

"It is a new reality, a problematic reality," settler spokesman Noam Arnon told Israel Television minutes before the opening. "It will be flooded with Arab cars which will pose a real danger to the Jews here."

Israeli and Palestinian workers cleared roadblocks on Sunday night. Some 80,000 Arabs live in the part of the town handed over to Palestinians. The town, the traditional burial place of the biblical Abraham, is holy to Moslems and Jews.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat had complained Israel was delaying opening the street. He and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are due to meet on Thursday to iron out various disputes.

Palestinian demands include the release of prisoners, an easing of restrictions on the flow of people and goods between Israel and the Palestinian territories, clearance for a Gaza airport to open and work to start on a Gaza seaport.

In Davos, Switzerland, Netanyahu defended his government on Sunday against Palestinian complaints, saying it had no objection to the Gaza seaport and airport as long as they met Israel's security requirements.
